38871:
2 Timothy is deeply rooted in Jewish family faith. Timothy's mother was a Jewish believer and his father a Greek (Acts 16:1), and Paul says that 'from childhood you have known the sacred writings' (2 Tim 3:15), the Jewish Scriptures taught at home, as Jewish mothers and grandmothers did. When Paul calls all Scripture 'God-breathed' (2 Tim 3:16), the Scriptures he means are primarily what Christians call the Old Testament, which Timothy learned from Lois and Eunice. Paul also says he serves God 'with a clear conscience, as did my ancestors' (2 Tim 1:3): he sees his faith in Christ as continuous with the faith of Israel.

The letter draws on Israel's stories. 'The Lord knows those who are his' (2 Tim 2:19) echoes Numbers 16:5, the Korah rebellion, where God distinguished true leaders from false. Jannes and Jambres, named as Moses' opponents (2 Tim 3:8), are the Egyptian magicians of Exodus 7 as named in Jewish tradition (they appear in the Damascus Document from Qumran and in the Targum). The pattern of a leader handing on his task resembles Moses and Joshua and Elijah and Elisha.

Traditional readers stress 2 Timothy's teaching on the authority and sufficiency of Scripture; critical readers see a later church consolidating its tradition. Both can agree that the letter places Christian teaching inside a Jewish family's handing-down of Israel's Scriptures, now read as making one 'wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus'.

38885: Paul's farewell, his loneliness and requests, and his confidence in the Lord's rescue into the heavenly kingdom.
38886: Handing on the faith in the face of death
38907: Breathed out by God. A rare word, perhaps coined for this verse; it expresses Scripture's divine origin and is followed by its usefulness for teaching and training.
38909: To share in suffering with someone; Paul invites Timothy to join him in the gospel's hardship.
38910: What has been entrusted for safekeeping: the gospel, guarded by the Holy Spirit.
38912: A visible manifestation, used of Christ's first coming and his future return; a word also used for gods and emperors appearing.
38914: Reliable. 'The saying is trustworthy', a formula found in the Pastorals, and 'if we are faithless, he remains faithful'.
38915: Moses' farewell charge to Joshua is the model for a leader's final instructions to a successor.
38916: Jannes and Jambres are traditional names for Pharaoh's magicians who opposed Moses.
38917: 'The Lord knows those who are his' recalls the Korah rebellion.
38918: Acts introduces Timothy, his Jewish mother and Greek father, and his joining Paul at Lystra.
38919: Paul also speaks of being poured out as a drink offering and of pressing on in a race.
38920: The gospel Paul guards is 'Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David' (2 Tim 2:8), who 'abolished death and brought life and immortality to light' (2 Tim 1:10) and who will judge the living and the dead at his appearing (2 Tim 4:1). The early saying 'if we have died with him, we will also live with him... if we are faithless, he remains faithful' (2 Tim 2:11-13) roots endurance in Christ's own faithfulness. For Jewish readers the Davidic Messiah and the resurrection are recognisable hopes; the letter claims they have begun in Jesus.
38921: 2 Timothy 3:16 as a ready-made statement about the 66-book Bible
38922: 2 Timothy 3:16 proves that the whole Bible, Old and New Testaments, is inspired and inerrant, and settles questions about which books belong in it.
38923: When this letter was written, the New Testament had not been collected. The 'sacred writings' Timothy knew from childhood (2 Tim 3:15) were the Jewish Scriptures. Paul's point is practical: Scripture makes one wise for salvation through faith in Christ and equips for good works. The emphasis is on Scripture's purpose and usefulness. Scholars across traditions (Luke Timothy Johnson, Philip Towner) agree on this.
38924: Evangelical scholars (B. B. Warfield historically; today William Mounce, Kevin Vanhoozer) agree the primary reference is the Old Testament, but argue that the principle applies to the apostolic writings, which the early church soon recognised as Scripture (1 Tim 5:18 quotes a saying of Jesus as Scripture; 2 Pet 3:16 places Paul's letters among 'the other Scriptures'). They hold that 'God-breathed' grounds Scripture's full truthfulness. The popular error is not the doctrine but ignoring the original reference and purpose.
38925: Remembering that Paul meant Israel's Scriptures honours the Old Testament as Christian Scripture, and keeping its purpose in view stops the verse being used only in arguments.
38926: A young leader facing opposition, desertions and the loss of his mentor was urged to courage, to faithful handling of Scripture and to making disciples who would make disciples.
38927: 2 Timothy speaks to mentoring and leadership succession, to believers tempted to be ashamed of Christ in a hostile culture, and to anyone facing death with faith. Its picture of a lonely old man asking for his coat and books makes the call to faithfulness very human.
38928: Instructions for organising new churches on Crete so that their leaders, households and public conduct 'adorn' the gospel of the God who saved them by mercy, not by their works.
38929: Presented as Paul writing to Titus, a Greek co-worker who had been with him in Jerusalem (Gal 2:1-3) and his trusted envoy to Corinth (2 Cor 8:23). Paul had left him on Crete to finish organising the churches (Titus 1:5).
38930: The letter claims Paul and shares the vocabulary, church order and concerns of 1 Timothy. The same arguments for and against Pauline authorship apply. Paul's visit to Crete is not recorded in Acts, beyond a brief stop at Fair Havens as a prisoner (Acts 27:7-13), so if Pauline it is usually placed after a release from Rome.
38931: Unknown; possibly on the way to Nicopolis
38932: Paul plans to winter at Nicopolis, probably the city in Epirus on the western coast of Greece, and asks Titus to join him there (Titus 3:12). Where he was when writing is not stated.
38933: Titus, overseeing young churches in the towns of Crete
38934: Churches existed in several towns but had no appointed elders. 'Insubordinate, empty talkers', especially 'of the circumcision party', were teaching 'Jewish myths' and human commandments for profit and 'upsetting whole families' (Titus 1:10-14).
38935: Rome completes the conquest of Crete; it later forms one province with Cyrene in North Africa, governed from Gortyn.
38936: Jews from Crete are among the pilgrims at Pentecost in Jerusalem (Acts 2:11; approximate date).
38937: Paul's prison ship shelters at Fair Havens on Crete before the storm (Acts 27:7-13; approximate date).
38938: Traditional date of Titus if written by Paul between imprisonments.
38939: Approximate date if the Pastorals are pseudonymous.
38940:
Crete is a large, mountainous island south of Greece, with dozens of towns; Homer called it the island of a hundred cities. After the Roman conquest in 67 BC it was joined administratively with Cyrene in Libya and governed from Gortyn. Crete had a Jewish community (Cretans were present at Pentecost, Acts 2:11, and Philo mentions Jews on Crete), which may explain the 'circumcision party' among the teachers.

Cretans had a poor reputation in the ancient world. The verb 'to Cretanise' meant to lie, and Cretans were mocked for claiming that Zeus, the immortal god, had a tomb on their island. Titus quotes one of their own 'prophets': 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons' (Titus 1:12). From at least Clement of Alexandria onwards this line has been attributed to the sixth-century BC poet Epimenides of Knossos, and the same poem may lie behind 'in him we live and move and have our being' (Acts 17:28). The quotation is part of the famous 'liar paradox'.

The letter is short but structured around one idea: sound teaching must produce good works that make the gospel attractive to outsiders. Elders must be blameless household managers (Titus 1:6-9). Older men and women, younger men and women, and slaves are each given instructions 'so that the word of God may not be reviled' (Titus 2:5) and so that 'in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour' (Titus 2:10). Then come two of the richest summaries of grace in the New Testament (Titus 2:11-14, Titus 3:4-7), which ground all this behaviour in what God has done.
38942: Cretans were proverbial liars in Greek literature. The letter uses a Cretan poet's own stereotype to rebuke the false teachers, not to condemn all Cretans, since the churches themselves are Cretan.
38944: Outsiders judged new groups by whether they disrupted households. The letter's household instructions aim to remove grounds for slander against the gospel.
38946: 'Saviour' (sōtēr) and 'appearing' (epiphaneia) were titles and words for gods and emperors who brought benefits. Titus applies them to God and to Jesus Christ.
38948: Civic life prized public benefaction. Believers are to be 'zealous for good works' and ready for every good work, a public goodness that blesses the town.
38950: Each town's church needed recognised leaders; the elder is described as 'God's steward' (oikonomos), a household manager entrusted with the master's goods.
38951:
Titus has a Jewish backbone beneath its Greek vocabulary. Its opening speaks of God's promise of eternal life made 'before the ages began' and revealed at the proper time (Titus 1:2-3). Its description of Christ who 'gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession' (Titus 2:14) quotes Israel's covenant identity: 'a people for his treasured possession' (Exod 19:5, Deut 14:2) and God's promise to redeem Israel from all its iniquities (Ps 130:8) and cleanse them (Ezek 37:23). The Gentile churches of Crete are being given Israel's own titles.

The 'washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us richly' (Titus 3:5-6) echoes Ezekiel's promise of sprinkling with clean water and a new spirit (Ezek 36:25-27) and Joel's outpouring of the Spirit (Joel 2:28).

The criticism of 'Jewish myths' and 'those of the circumcision' (Titus 1:10, Titus 1:14) has to be read carefully. These are teachers within the church, perhaps Jewish believers or Gentiles drawn to Jewish-style speculation and purity rules, who taught that some things were unclean (Titus 1:15). The letter's reply, 'to the pure, all things are pure', is about food and purity rules imposed on Gentiles. It is a dispute within the Jesus movement, not a judgment on Judaism.
38953: Paul greets Titus with a statement of the hope of eternal life promised before time.
38955: In every town, appoint blameless, hospitable, self-controlled elders who hold to sound teaching.
38957: Rebuke teachers who upset households for profit with myths and purity rules.
38959: Each group in the household of faith lives so that the word is not reviled.
38961: God's grace has appeared, training us to live godly lives as we await Christ's appearing.
38963: Be good citizens, for God saved us not by works but by mercy, through the Spirit's renewing.
38965: Avoid foolish controversies, warn the divisive, and help travelling workers.
38966: Sound teaching that adorns the gospel
38985: God's gift that saves and also trains (paideuousa) believers to live new lives.

38989: Applied six times in this short letter, three to God and three to Jesus Christ.
38991: New birth or renewal; used by Stoics for the rebirth of the world, and in Matthew for the renewal of all things. Here it is a personal new beginning by the Spirit.
38993: A classic Greek virtue of moderation and good sense, asked of every group in the church.
38994: Closely parallel instructions on elders, false teachers and household conduct.
38995: 'A people for his own possession' echoes God's covenant words at Sinai.
38996: Washing and the gift of a new spirit recall Ezekiel's promise of cleansing.
38997: Titus himself was the uncircumcised Greek not compelled to be circumcised in Jerusalem.
38998: Cretans at Pentecost and Paul's stop at Fair Havens are Crete's other New Testament appearances.
38999: Titus contains one of the clearest New Testament statements of Jesus' divinity: believers wait for 'the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ' (Titus 2:13), which most scholars read as calling Jesus 'God', though some take it as two persons, 'the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ'. Christ gave himself to redeem and purify a people. The title 'Saviour' moves back and forth between God and Jesus in the letter, presenting the Father and Son as acting together in salvation. Jewish readers will recognise the language of redemption and a treasured people from Israel's own Scriptures.
39000: 'Cretans are always liars' as a licence for ethnic stereotypes
39001: Titus 1:12 shows that some peoples have fixed bad characters, and the Bible endorses judging nations by their reputations.
39002: The letter quotes a Cretan poet's own proverb as a rhetorical jab at specific false teachers who were deceiving for money. The churches that receive the letter are Cretan, and the letter expects Cretan elders to be blameless and Cretan believers to be transformed by grace (Titus 2:11-12). Ancient rhetoric often turned a group's proverb against its own members. Commentators (Towner, Mounce, Johnson) note the rebuke is aimed so 'that they may be sound in the faith' (Titus 1:13).
39003: Evangelical commentators accept that 'this testimony is true' affirms the poet's point about these teachers' behaviour but not a racial theory. Some acknowledge that the sentence sounds harsh to modern ears and should not be used to label any people. There is little scholarly dispute.
39004: The gospel in Titus transforms Cretans; using the verse to stereotype others contradicts the letter's own message of grace for 'all people' (Titus 2:11).
39005: 'Washing of regeneration' (Titus 3:5): baptism or the Spirit's inner work?
39006: Evangelicals often read Titus 3:5 as describing only an inner, spiritual cleansing at conversion, with no reference to baptism. Others (sacramental traditions) read it as stating that baptism itself regenerates.
39007: Most commentators, including evangelicals such as Gordon Fee and Philip Towner, think baptism is at least in view, because 'washing' was the obvious early Christian word for baptism (compare Eph 5:26, Acts 22:16). In the Jewish background, washing is linked with the Spirit's renewal (Ezek 36:25-27). The emphasis falls on God's mercy and the Spirit, not on human action.
39008: Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran theologians read the verse as teaching baptismal regeneration, with God acting through the water. Reformed and Baptist evangelicals argue that baptism is the sign of a regeneration worked by the Spirit, and that the verse's 'not by works' guards against treating any rite as automatic. This is a long-standing difference between traditions; see /debates/baptism.
39009: The verse holds together outward sign and inner renewal; each tradition has to account for both.
39010: Young churches on an island with a bad reputation learned that God's grace could produce trustworthy leaders and households whose goodness would silence slander.
39011: Titus speaks to church planting and leadership, to the link between belief and behaviour, and to Christian witness through ordinary good citizenship. Its short summaries of grace (Titus 2:11-14, Titus 3:4-7) are among the best one-paragraph statements of the gospel.
39012: A one-page letter in which a prisoner asks a householder to receive back his slave Onesimus 'no longer as a slave but more than a slave, as a beloved brother', putting the gospel to work inside a household church.
39013: Paul in prison, calling himself 'an old man' (or possibly 'an ambassador', Phlm 1:9) and a 'prisoner of Christ Jesus'. He had led Philemon to faith (Phlm 1:19) and now Onesimus too (Phlm 1:10).
39014: Undisputed. Its personal character, lack of doctrinal agenda and close links to Colossians' greetings make forgery very unlikely. It was in Marcion's collection (c. 140) and the Muratorian list.
39015: Paul asks Philemon to prepare a guest room for him (Phlm 1:22). That is easier to imagine from Ephesus, about 190 km (120 miles) from Colossae, than from Rome, over 1,600 km away, and a runaway or a slave seeking a mediator could more easily reach Ephesus. Rome is the traditional view, supported by the link with Colossians. Coordinates show Ephesus.
39016: Philemon, with Apphia, Archippus and the church in his house
39017: Onesimus, Philemon's slave, had left his master's house, perhaps owing him something (Phlm 1:18), and had come to Paul, become a believer and served Paul. Paul now sends him back with this letter and with Tychicus (Col 4:7-9). The letter is addressed to the whole house church, so Philemon will respond in public.
39018: Spartacus' slave revolt in Italy (73-71 BC), a lasting memory of what Romans feared from slaves.
39019: Date of Philemon if written from an Ephesian imprisonment.
39020: Date of Philemon if written from Rome; in the same year the Roman senate executes all 400 slaves of the murdered city prefect Pedanius Secundus (Tacitus, Annals 14.42-45).
39021: Ignatius of Antioch mentions a bishop of Ephesus named Onesimus (Ignatius, To the Ephesians 1.3); some scholars speculate he is the same man (approximate date).
39022:
Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world. Perhaps one in five or six people in the empire was enslaved, and in cities the proportion could be higher. Slaves were legal property. They did every kind of work, from mining and farm labour to teaching and managing businesses, and some were later freed. A slave who ran away (a fugitivus) could be hunted down, branded or punished severely, and anyone who harboured him could be liable for the owner's losses.

However, Roman legal writers also distinguish a runaway from a slave who went to a friend of the master (an amicus domini) to plead for help after a quarrel or mistake; such a slave was not legally a fugitive. Peter Lampe (1985) and Brian Rapske argued that Onesimus fits this case better: he went to Paul, his master's respected friend, to seek mediation. A famous parallel is the letter of Pliny the Younger to his friend Sabinianus (Letters 9.21), asking him to forgive a freedman who had come to Pliny in tears. Other scholars (John Barclay, Douglas Moo) still think Onesimus probably fled, and Allen Callahan has argued, as a minority view, that Onesimus was Philemon's estranged brother and not a slave at all, reading 'brother both in the flesh and in the Lord' (Phlm 1:16) literally.

Paul's letter is a masterpiece of persuasion. He could command but chooses to appeal 'for love's sake' (Phlm 1:8-9). He plays on Onesimus' name, which means 'useful': 'formerly he was useless to you, but now he is useful' (Phlm 1:11). He offers to pay any debt in his own handwriting, then reminds Philemon that he owes Paul his very self (Phlm 1:19). And he asks for 'even more than I say' (Phlm 1:21), which many read as a hint about freedom or about sending Onesimus back to serve Paul.
39024: Slaves belonged to the household (familia) under the master's authority. They could be punished, sold or freed at the owner's will. Household churches therefore had masters and slaves worshipping side by side.
39026: A slave in trouble could go to a friend of the owner to ask for intercession without being legally a runaway. Many scholars think Onesimus did this.
39028: Letters asking one friend to receive another kindly were common. Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul himself.
39030: Paul writes a legally recognisable promise in his own hand: 'I will repay it'. In the honour economy he also reminds Philemon of the debt he owes Paul.
39031: Public reading in the house church
39032: The letter is addressed to the church in Philemon's house, so it was read aloud before the community, including other slaves. Philemon's response would be watched by everyone.
39034: Paul calls Philemon his partner and Onesimus his own 'heart' and child. Kinship language turns a legal relationship into a family one.
39035:
Philemon does not quote Scripture, but its moral world draws on Israel's Torah. The Law limited the enslavement of fellow Israelites and required their release in the seventh year (Exod 21:2, Deut 15:12-15), reminding Israel, 'you were a slave in the land of Egypt and the LORD your God redeemed you'. Most strikingly, Deuteronomy commanded: 'You shall not give up to his master a slave who has escaped from his master to you. He shall dwell with you... you shall not wrong him' (Deut 23:15-16). This was very unusual in the ancient Near East. Paul, as a Jew, sends Onesimus back not to bondage but with an appeal that he be received as a brother, which in Israel's terms is the way a fellow member of the covenant family is treated (Lev 25:39-43).

The letter also uses Jewish ideas of household and brotherhood. Paul is a 'father' to Onesimus (Phlm 1:10), as rabbis spoke of teachers as fathers to their disciples. The church is one family where the deepest relationship is 'in the Lord'.

Interpreters differ on how far the letter challenges slavery. Some (Norman Petersen, N. T. Wright) see it as subtly undermining the master-slave relationship from within by making it impossible to treat a brother as property. Others (Jennifer Glancy, J. Albert Harrill) argue that early Christians generally accepted slavery as a given and that the letter must not be romanticised. African American interpreters (Allen Callahan, Lisa Bowens) have shown how the letter was used both by slaveholders and by abolitionists.
39037: Paul, a prisoner, greets Philemon, Apphia, Archippus and the whole house church.
39039: Philemon has refreshed the saints; Paul prays his partnership will be effective.
39041: On the basis of love Paul appeals for his child Onesimus, once useless, now useful.
39043: Perhaps he was parted for a while so Philemon could have him back forever as a beloved brother.
39045: Paul will pay any debt, though Philemon owes him his own self.
39047: Paul hopes to visit; greetings from his fellow workers.
39064: Shared life in Christ, which Paul hopes will be 'effective' in how Philemon acts.
